e.t: This word means “pail,” referring to a container used for holding or carrying something. It is a noun, so it names the object itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage uses the pail.

Adli is a proper name, appearing as “Adli; Athli” in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:29. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the person’s particular role cannot be described from the name alone.

This word means “sing.” It is a verb describing the act of making music with the voice. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 70 times, including frequent use in Psalms and other passages connected with worship, praise, or public celebration. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to sing, whether the word describes an individual or a group. The surrounding passage determines what is being sung and why, but the word itself identifies vocal music or song.

This verb means being “ashamed to do” something. It describes a person’s feeling toward carrying out an action, presenting shame as the reason for not wanting to do it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs five times: once in Proverbs and four times in 2 and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means a ray or beam: a line of light or radiant energy extending outward. It can describe a visible streak coming from a source, or a beam shining across space. In this LXX corpus, the word appears three times, in Wisdom and Sirach. Its basic sense is concrete and visual; the surrounding verse determines how the ray or beam functions in that passage. The word names the ray itself rather than describing an action.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Anatolē” or “Anatoli,” rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It identifies a named entity within the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The word occurs 167 times in the Greek LXX corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion. Its precise reference—whether to a person, place, or other named subject—depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “forbearance” or “patient endurance”: the ability to bear difficulty, injury, or opposition without giving way to anger or retaliation. It describes steady restraint rather than weakness or indifference. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Wisdom 2:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the deliberate endurance of hardship while continuing to stand firm.

This noun means “support” or “prop”: something that holds up, steadies, or strengthens. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Psalms 17:19 and Ezekiel 30:6. Its basic sense is practical and concrete, describing a source of stability rather than an abstract idea. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to a physical support or uses that image to describe something that gives strength.

This Greek LXX verb means to force someone or something away. It describes active removal rather than merely leaving or moving aside, so it presents the action of driving away by pressure or strength. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Proverbs 22:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains compelling something away from its place or position.

This LXX Greek noun means “perplexity”: a state of being confused, troubled, or unable to see a clear way forward. It names inward uncertainty or distress rather than a physical object or action. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including passages in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a troubled lack of clarity or direction.

This LXX word is a proper name, given as “Aradios; Arathios.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. The name appears three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Genesis and twice in Ezekiel. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular referent cannot be identified here, but its basic role is to designate a named individual, group, or place in those passages.

Asbel is a proper name, referring to a person named Asbel, also represented as Azvil. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs twice: once in Genesis 46:21 and once in 1 Chronicles 8:1. These references place it among genealogical names, but the name itself does not express an action, quality, or doctrine. Its ordinary function is simply to identify an individual within Israel’s family records.

This verb means to act in an irreverent way—to show a lack of proper respect or reverence. It describes conduct rather than a person or object, presenting irreverence as something someone does. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs 33 times, showing that this is a recurring description of wrongful or disrespectful behavior. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “gladly”: it describes an action done with willingness, pleasure, or readiness rather than reluctance. It tells how someone acts, adding the sense that the person is pleased or willing to do what is being described. The word occurs three times in the LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a willing, pleased manner of action.

Achilid, also written Akhilith, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It functions as a personal or identifying name in the Greek Old Testament text and is not presented with an additional lexical definition. The name occurs twice in the Septuagint, both times in 1 Kings, at 1 Kings 4:3 and 1 Kings 4:12. Its precise reference in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Baithzacharia, also rendered Vethzakharia, is a proper name for a place rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice, both times in 1 Maccabees 6, in verses 32 and 33. The name itself identifies a location; its specific importance and role must be understood from the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Benōr, also rendered Venor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:8. The available information identifies it as the name’s lexical form but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which person it identifies or what role that person has in the passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal name, with the exact identity determined by the context of 1 Kings 4:8.

This word means “3” and identifies the number three; it is also connected with the name “gimel.” It functions as a number designation rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:17. The available lexical information supports its numerical meaning, while the isolated reference does not provide enough verse text to explain any further contextual force.

This verb means “trace genealogy”: to follow or set out a person’s family line through successive generations. It describes the action of tracing ancestry, rather than naming one particular family member. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 5:1. The word identifies a genealogical tracing action; the surrounding passage determines the specific purpose and emphasis of that action.

This word means “sweet,” describing something pleasant to taste. As an adjective, it identifies the quality of a substance rather than naming the substance itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 9:17. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used simply for taste or as part of a comparison. The word therefore points to pleasant sweetness in the thing being described.

This word means “load” or “cargo”—something carried, transported, or borne as a burden. It is a noun describing the material being carried rather than the act of carrying it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Exodus 23:5 and 2 Kings 5:17. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a physical load or shipment. The two approved meanings, “load” and “cargo,” express the same basic sense.

This word is a proper name, given as “Dalouia” or “Thaloia.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 3:3. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not explain whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “expense”: money or resources spent for a purpose. It refers to the cost involved in carrying out an undertaking, rather than to the undertaking itself. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Ezra and several deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains expenditure or cost.

This Greek LXX verb means “frighten”: to cause someone to become afraid. It describes an action directed toward another person rather than fear experienced inwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 20:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of making someone afraid. The word is therefore useful for recognizing language about producing fear or discouragement in another person.

This word describes something that is completely or thoroughly empty. As a noun, it refers to emptiness rather than merely expressing that something contains little. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 21:5, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The phrase “quite empty” captures the word’s central sense: an absence of contents, resources, or fullness, depending on what the surrounding passage identifies as empty.

This LXX Greek verb means “fly through”: it describes movement swiftly across or through a space. Its wording presents passing through in flight rather than merely traveling or crossing on foot. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including Psalms, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains movement through the air.

This Greek LXX noun means “justice”—what is right, fair, and properly judged. It can describe justice as a quality, a standard by which actions are assessed, or the rightful judgment carried out against wrongdoing. The word appears 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, showing that it is used across legal, poetic, wisdom, and historical settings. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains justice and right judgment.

Dorymenes is a proper personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also given as “Thorimenis.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. Because no surrounding verse text is provided, the name’s particular role in either passage cannot be stated beyond identifying it as a person’s name.

This word means “close,” describing something or someone that is near in position or relationship. It can function in a sentence to point out proximity, whether used to describe a location, a person, or the nearness of an event or time. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 46 times across 45 verses, including passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is described as close and the surrounding sentence.

Edram, also rendered Ethram, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Kings 2:46. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no surrounding verse text, its personal identity and significance must be determined from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “bring in”: it describes causing a person or thing to enter or be brought inside. Its basic sense is movement into a place, situation, or gathering, with the surrounding sentence showing what is brought and where it goes. The word occurs 93 times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare technical term. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.h: Show Forth or Bring to Light
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “shew forth” or “bring to light”—to make something known, visible, or clear. It describes the act of revealing what was hidden or making a matter understandable. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, especially in Sirach and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being revealed and how the surrounding sentence presents it.

This noun refers to an “elephant” or to “ivory,” the valuable material associated with that animal. Its precise sense is determined by how it functions in the surrounding sentence: it can name the living creature or the substance made from its tusks. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:35. No broader scriptural pattern is available from its single occurrence, but its basic meaning is clear as either the animal or ivory material.

This Greek LXX adjective means “dumbfounded,” describing someone left astonished and unable to respond normally. It expresses a striking state of amazement rather than an action or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once each in Proverbs, Isaiah, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains a person overcome with astonishment.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something as special or distinguishing—set apart from what is ordinary or readily confused with other things. It can identify a person, object, or quality by emphasizing its notable difference or particular character. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is clear, while the surrounding sentence determines what makes the person or thing distinctive in each occurrence. It is rendered here by the meaning “special; distinguishing.”

This adjective describes someone or something that is “in want of” something. It points to a condition of need or lack, with the surrounding sentence showing what is wanted. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, both in Sirach. Its basic meaning remains focused on being in want of something rather than naming the particular thing involved. The precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This noun refers to “small grapes left for gleaners”—the few grapes remaining after a vineyard harvest for people to gather. It names what is overlooked or left behind rather than the main crop. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Judges, Lamentations, Obadiah, Micah, and Zephaniah. The word therefore carries a concrete picture of harvest remnants, while its precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun can mean a “saying,” referring to something spoken or expressed in words. Its recorded meaning also includes “almost,” though the surrounding sentence determines how that sense functions. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 44:5. Because the verse text is not included here, this summary gives the word’s ordinary lexical range rather than explaining its particular use in that verse.

This word means “hostility”: an attitude or condition of active opposition or ill will toward another. As a noun, it names such hostility; as an adjective, it can describe something marked by hostility. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across Proverbs, Micah, and 1 Maccabees. Its appearances in Proverbs 32:10, Micah 7:8, Micah 7:10, and 1 Maccabees 11:12 show that it is used in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical Greek writings, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being described.

Zabdia is a personal name, also rendered “Zavthia.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Ezra: once in Ezra 8:8 and once in Ezra 10:20. The available name forms indicate that “Zabdia” and “Zavthia” are variant renderings of the same personal name, while the surrounding verse text is needed to identify the particular person in each occurrence.

This adjective means “enviable”: worthy of admiration or desire because of a favorable quality or condition. Its sense is positive, describing what others may rightly regard with longing or esteem; it does not name the sinful feeling of envy itself. In this LXX corpus, it occurs four times across Genesis, Exodus, and the books of Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what makes the person or thing enviable.

This verb means “kindle into flame; light up”—to cause something to begin burning or to make it shine brightly. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the action of igniting or rekindling something rather than merely observing a flame. It occurs four times in the Septuagint, all in two verses of 2 Kings 8 (2 Kings 8:1, 5). Its precise force depends on the surrounding context.

Thabor is a proper name, rendered “Thabōr” or “Thavor,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named place or designation. It occurs seven times across seven verses, with several occurrences in Judges and additional occurrences in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and Psalms. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun refers to someone who has been castrated, that is, a eunuch. It describes a person by a physical condition rather than naming an action or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 22:24 and Deuteronomy 23:2. Those references show its use within the Old Testament Greek translation, while the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s basic meaning remains a castrated man or eunuch.

This verb means “make to sit down” or “seat” someone. It describes the action of causing a person to take a seated position, rather than simply sitting by choice. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears once, in 4 Maccabees 17:3. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the placing or settling of someone in a seated position. It is a practical action word, focused on causing someone to sit.

This word means “16” and identifies the numerical value sixteen. “Ayin” is included as the label associated with that number. It functions as an indeclinable number rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Psalm 118:121. Its precise role there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the number sixteen.

Iphina, also rendered “Ifina,” is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It occurs once in the LXX, in 1 Chronicles 7:38. Because this is a personal name rather than a common word, it does not describe an action, quality, or relationship by itself. Its precise significance in that genealogy depends on the surrounding verse and family listing, which are not included here.

“Iōra” or “Iora” is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 2:18. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its personal identity and role must be learned from that context. The word itself functions simply as a personal name.

Karnain, also given as Karnen, is a proper name used for a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. The supplied lexical meaning identifies the name but does not provide a broader descriptive sense. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Genesis and three times in 1 Maccabees. Its precise referent in any passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means “mix up; mingle the ingredients.” It describes combining separate ingredients so they become mingled together rather than remaining distinct. As a verb, it expresses an action of mixing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 28:14; its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense is the bringing together of ingredients by mixing them.

This noun describes a state of “stupefying” or “bewilderment”—a condition in which a person is overcome with confusion or stunned inability to respond clearly. Its central idea is mental disorientation rather than a specific action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Psalm 59:5 and Isaiah 29:10. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force it carries in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “make sure” or describes something as “made fast.” It refers to securing, fastening, or making something firm. As a verb, it describes an action someone performs or the resulting condition of something secured, rather than naming a person, object, or abstract quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in 3 Maccabees 4:9. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “force down” or “prevail”: to overcome resistance, gain the upper hand, or become stronger than an opposing person or force. It describes effective dominance rather than merely attempting to act. The word appears 94 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this corpus, so its basic sense applies across many situations involving strength, opposition, or victory. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, given as “Kedem” or “Kethem.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action or quality, though the specific referent must be determined from the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Jeremiah and twice in Ezekiel. Its use is limited and name-like, so its central meaning is the designation itself rather than a broad concept or repeated biblical theme.

The word means “cake,” referring to a prepared food and functioning as a noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in 2 Samuel. It names a food item rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word may refer to one cake or more than one, depending on the sentence. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a cake or cakes.

This verb means “hang”: to suspend someone or something, or to place it in a hanging position. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 33 times. Its uses include people being hung and objects or structures described as hanging, so the basic idea is physical suspension rather than a specialized religious meaning. The surrounding verse determines whether the word describes an execution, a public display, or an ordinary position. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to camphor or henna, a fragrant plant or substance. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the word’s precise reference in each passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a name for camphor or henna rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This adjective describes something frivolous or silly—something lacking seriousness or sound purpose. It characterizes a person, action, statement, or matter as foolishly light rather than weighty or sensible. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:44. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding context, but its ordinary sense is clear: it marks something as trivial, foolish, or unserious.

This Greek LXX verb means “bear,” referring to bringing forth a child. As a verb, it describes the act of giving birth rather than the child, the mother, or the surrounding circumstances. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, appearing once in Genesis and once in Psalms. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of bearing or bringing forth. The word therefore points to childbirth in a direct, action-focused way.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Masphe” or “Masfe.” It functions as a name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:19. The available information identifies its name-form and location in the text, but does not provide enough surrounding verse context to explain more about the person, place, or thing named there.

This adverb means “gloriously” or “with great glory.” It describes an action carried out in a splendid, exalted, or honor-filled manner, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 6:39. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic contribution is to show that something is done with great glory or magnificence.

Mesraim, also rendered Mezrem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Genesis, appearing in Genesis 10:6 and Genesis 10:13. Its precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding genealogical context, but the lexical meaning supplied for the name is simply "Mesraim; Mezrem."

This noun means “crescent,” referring to something shaped like the curved portion of the moon. It is a precise word for a curved, partly illuminated form rather than a broad term for any circular object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Judges and Isaiah, including references to crescents as objects. The surrounding verse determines exactly what kind of crescent is meant in each passage.

μηχανάομαι means “prepare” or “make ready.” It is a verb describing an action that brings something into readiness. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, making it an uncommon word in this corpus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains preparation or making something ready for what follows.

This Greek word means “remember” or “remind”: it describes bringing something to mind, keeping it in memory, or calling it back to someone’s attention. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for both human remembering and being reminded of God’s words, acts, or covenant. It occurs 102 times, so it is a broadly used verb rather than a rare or specialized term. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 9:15, and it continues through 4 Maccabees 13:12.

Michas is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also represented as “Mikhas,” reflecting the same named person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 23:20. Because it is a proper noun, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes one person from others in the biblical record, rather than expressing a general idea or instruction.

Mosoch, also written Mosokh, is a proper name used to identify a named people or figure in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact referent in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

“Neemia” is a proper name, the Greek LXX form associated with Nehemiah. It identifies a person by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs four times in the Greek LXX, all in the book of Nehemiah, from Nehemiah 1:1 through Nehemiah 12:26. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic function is simply to name Nehemiah.

gl: hinder; belonging to the hinder part
d: hinder; belonging to the hinder part

e.t: This adjective means “hinder; belonging to the hinder part,” describing something situated toward the back or rear. It is used for a rear section or part rather than for a person’s character or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle and temple furnishings, and also in prophetic passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the object or place it describes.

gl: as much as; as many as
d: as much as; as many as

e.t: This Greek LXX word means “as much as” or “as many as.” It is an adjective or pronoun that indicates an amount or number, often connecting one quantity with another. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to things measured in bulk or to multiple people or objects. The word occurs 547 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it serves as a broad quantity-and-comparison term rather than naming one particular kind of thing. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding words.

This Greek LXX preposition means “from; by.” It marks a point of origin or indicates association with, proximity to, or action connected with someone or something. Its exact sense depends on the words and passage around it, but the central idea is movement or connection in relation to a source or person. It is common throughout the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, occurring 769 times in this LXX corpus. It appears from Genesis through Susanna, showing broad use rather than a meaning limited to one setting.

This verb means “relaxed.” It describes something being loosened or becoming less tightly held, tense, or constrained. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition involving release from tightness or strain rather than a fixed object or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what was relaxed in that occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “arrest; catch.” It describes taking hold of someone or something so that it is seized or captured. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Song of Songs 2:15. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely how this action functions in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “pain”—physical or inward distress that a person experiences. It names the hurt or hardship itself rather than an action. The word occurs 70 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it can describe recurring human suffering in many settings. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This word means “Sabbath eve”. It is a noun referring to the time immediately before the Sabbath. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalm 92:1, so its meaning is narrow and specific rather than a broad description of Sabbath observance. The word identifies a particular day or time in relation to the Sabbath. Its precise significance in Psalm 92:1 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the basic meaning remains clear: the eve, or day before, the Sabbath.

This noun refers to refining or burning—the process or experience of being subjected to heat for purification or intense burning. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Proverbs 34:21 and Amos 4:9. Those references show its limited distribution, but without the verse text they do not establish the particular force in either passage. Its central idea is heat applied in a refining or burning process; the surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis is purification, the burning itself, or its result.

Rodokos, also called Rhothokos, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Within the LXX corpus, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 13:21. The name itself does not express a general idea or everyday concept; it serves to identify someone. The person’s identity and role must be understood from the verse and its surrounding passage, rather than from the name alone.

Sadaiem, also rendered Satheem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which kind of named entity it designates. This name occurs once, in 1 Samuel 24:3. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the name itself supplies identification rather than a broader descriptive meaning.

Salabin, also rendered Salavin, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 19:42. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be explained further here, but its basic function is clear: it is a personal or place name recorded in the biblical narrative or list.

Samath is a proper name, referring to someone identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Chronicles 24:26, and its meaning is preserved simply as “Samath.” Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name should not be given an additional meaning or symbolic significance. It functions as a personal designation rather than as a description, action, quality, or general concept.

Selēk, also rendered Selik, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:39. Because the word functions as a personal name, its basic meaning is the individual it identifies; the name itself does not supply an additional description or spiritual idea. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in the passage.
